plan.title: Alan Turing: The Man Who Taught Machines to Think
plan.description: Alan Turing (1912-1954) was a British mathematician who broke Nazi codes and laid the foundations of computer science and artificial intelligence. His story ends in injustice, and a pardon that came decades too late.

beats.narration: He helped break Nazi codes, imagined the modern computer, and asked whether machines could think. Then his own country convicted him. This is the story of Alan Turing.
beats.speaker: narrator

beats.narration: Alan Turing was born on June 23, 1912, in Paddington, London. His parents worked in India, so he spent much of his childhood fostered in English homes, often lonely.
beats.speaker: narrator

beats.narration: At King's College, Cambridge, his mind flourished. At just twenty-two, he was elected a Fellow because of the strength of his dissertation. Cambridge gave him his first real home.
beats.speaker: narrator

beats.narration: In 1936, he introduced the universal computing machine, now called the Turing machine. His idea: one machine, given the right instructions, could compute anything. That idea underpins modern computers.

props.text: One machine, given the right instructions, could compute anything.

beats.speaker: narrator

beats.narration: Then war came. First, the Turing machine idea of a general-purpose thinking engine. Second, the Enigma, Germany's coded messages. Third, the messages decoded at Bletchley Park, which saved lives.
beats.speaker: narrator

beats.narration: At Bletchley Park, Britain's top-secret codebreaking centre, Turing played a pivotal role in decrypting German army intelligence messages. Machines and mathematics did what no one person could.
beats.speaker: narrator

beats.narration: The work continued with engineer Tommy Flowers, who built Colossus. Many consider it the world's first operational computer. It helped read the German Geheimschreiber, a cipher that used many rotors.
beats.speaker: narrator

beats.narration: After the war, Turing turned to the brain. He gave the first public lecture on artificial intelligence, and in 1948 designed an early learning neural network. His employer rejected it.
beats.speaker: narrator

beats.narration: He also proposed the Turing test, a way to judge whether a machine can imitate a human. The question still shapes the debate about AI today.

props.definition: A criterion for judging whether a machine can think, by whether it can imitate a human.

beats.speaker: narrator

beats.narration: Near the end of his life, Turing was convicted for being homosexual and subjected to chemical castration. He died on June 7, 1954. A royal pardon came some sixty years later.
beats.speaker: narrator

beats.narration: The man Britain punished gave the world its computers and its questions about thinking machines. Every device you use carries his idea: one machine, endless possibilities.
beats.speaker: narrator

accuracy.reason: Mostly traceable to notes, but Beat 5 mangles the Enigma/Colossus story and says Turing 'imagined the modern computer'. Colossus is linked to Turing's circle without clarity. 'Fellow ... because of dissertation' is as in the notes.

coverage.reason: Covers the Turing machine, Bletchley, Colossus, Turing test, conviction, death and pardon. But there is nothing on how Enigma was actually broken (the Bombe), the conviction year is only on screen, and the pardon year 2013 is missing. Cause of death is omitted.

structure.reason: The chronological chapters are clear. Beat 5 is a confused, redundant 'First, Second, Third' that adds nothing, and the early-life beats get disproportionate time. The ending is rushed.

hook_ending.reason: The opening 'Then his own country convicted him' creates tension. The close, 'one machine, endless possibilities', is decent but slightly cliched.

tone.reason: Generally respectful, but the sensitive material is handled in flat, clinical wording ('convicted for being homosexual', 'subjected to chemical castration') with no human weight.

visuals.reason: Scene types vary (timeline, diagram, gallery, definition). But the diagram and the repeated generic 'researcher working at computer' clip are filler, and the timeline's 'Age 22' and '60 years on' entries are vague.

originality.reason: Largely a paraphrase of the notes; few vivid specifics, and nothing surprising beyond the rejected neural network.

instructions.reason: English, about the right length, and covers the basics. Missing 2013 and the 1952 date in speech, and the reviewer's key points are only partly met.
